{"problem": {"theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "proof_text": "Proof.  We think of the final “blocked’’ configuration as the result of tearing out \(b(n)\) disjoint 3-stamp blocks (each block either 3 in a row or 3 in a column) so that no further 3-stamp block remains.  Call any three consecutive positions in a row or in a column a “potential triple.’’  There are in all  
\[
H \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{horizontal triples,}
\qquad
V \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{vertical triples,}
\]
and hence 
\[
T \;=\;H+V \;=\;2\,n\,(n-2)
\]
potential triples that must each be “hit’’ (i.e.\ each must lose at least one stamp) by our removed blocks.

1.  Lower bound \(b(n)\ge \tfrac1{7}n^2-cn\).  
 
Fix any one of the \(b(n)\) removed blocks.  If it is a horizontal block occupying cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\), then it “hits’’ (i.e.\ destroys at least one cell of) at most
  •  all horizontal triples that include one of those three cells;  in a row of length \(n\), each interior cell lies in 3 horizontal triples and each end‐cell in 1 or 2, and one checks easily that the three consecutive cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\) together lie in at most 5 distinct horizontal triples;  
  •  all vertical triples that include one of those three cells;  each of the three removed stamps lies in at most 3 vertical triples, so altogether at most \(3\times3=9\) vertical triples.  
Hence that one horizontal block can destroy at most \(5+9=14\) of the \(T\) potential triples.  Likewise any vertical block destroys at most \(14\) potential triples.

14k≥2n(n-2),

n(m/5)≤n²/5.

n²/3≤n²/5+2n.

n²/7-(2/7)n≤b(n)≤n²/5+2n,

which proves the theorem.","reason":"The supplied upper construction is invalid: blocks C and E overlap, and its asserted coverage fails. {"problem": {"theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "candidate_text": "Let n be a positive integer. We prove the result with c=2/7 and d=2.

For n≥3, call each set of three consecutive cells in one row or column a potential triple. There are

T=2n(n-2)

potential triples. In any terminal configuration, every potential triple contains a removed stamp; otherwise those three stamps could be removed as another block.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal potential triples: their starting columns must lie within two positions of the block's starting column. Each of its three cells belongs to at most three vertical potential triples, so the block meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most 14 potential triples altogether. The same bound holds for a vertical block.

Consequently, if k blocks produce a terminal configuration, then

14k≥2n(n-2),

so

k≥n(n-2)/7=n²/7-2n/7.

This applies in particular to k=b(n). For n=1,2, we have b(n)=0, and the same inequality remains valid. Hence the lower bound holds with c=2/7.

For the upper bound, first suppose n≥5. Let m=5⌊n/5⌋ and r=n-m, so 0≤r≤4. In every row, partition the first m columns into consecutive groups of five. In each such group remove one horizontal block as follows:

• in every odd-numbered row, remove the first three cells of the group;
• in every even-numbered row, remove the last three cells of the group.

These blocks are pairwise disjoint, and their number is

n(m/5)≤n²/5.

No horizontal triple lying wholly in the first m columns remains, because in each row every run of unremoved cells there has length at most two. Moreover, no vertical triple in any of the first m columns remains: in positions 1 and 2 of each five-column group every odd row is removed, in position 3 every row is removed, and in positions 4 and 5 every even row is removed. Every three consecutive rows include both parities.

Therefore every triple still available after these removals lies entirely in the strip S consisting of columns m-1,m,…,n. Indeed, a horizontal triple not contained in the first m columns starts no earlier than column m-1, while an available vertical triple must have column greater than m. The strip has width r+2≤6.

Now repeatedly remove any available block until none remains. Removing stamps cannot create a new available triple, so every additional block lies in S. Since these additional blocks are disjoint and each uses three cells of S, their number is at most

|S|/3=(r+2)n/3≤2n.

Thus

b(n)≤n²/5+2n.

For 1≤n<5, a greedy maximal collection contains at most n²/3 blocks, and

n²/3≤n²/5+2n.

Hence the upper bound also holds for these n. Therefore, for every positive integer n,

n²/7-(2/7)n≤b(n)≤n²/5+2n,

which proves the theorem."}
